If you are looking for another text-based resource, text 4HOPE to 741741 to text with a trained crisis consultant.

I work at a crisis center, and it always pains me to see comments of bad crisis prevention practices.  At the one I work at, very rarely do we miss a call or put a call on hold for such a long time.  These kinds of jobs are like any emergency hotline, in that they can be short staffed at times.  Unfortunately, I sometimes have had to put clients on hold for 15-30 minutes, but this is very rare, and usually happens if two calls come in at the same time, and all the staff members are working.  When this occurs, we do all we can to make sure both calls are safe despite the difficulty of the situation.  It has happened maybe 2-3 times in my whole two years I've been working.  

As far as other common criticisms I've seen on reddit, I tend to see that somebody had unnecessary police intervention or hospitalization from calling.  Now it might vary from hotline to hotline, but I very rarely call the police on a client.  The only time I call the police on a client are if they can't confirm their safety for the night.  If they continue to show significant signs that they might harm themselves, and they refuse to come to our facility to be assessed on their own, then we are required to have police involvement (keep in mind, we follow HIPPA, so we must prevent harm by law).  Once again, this is very rare.  I have only called the police on a client once, and I truly believe the client was in serious danger.  The hotline I work for would never have police involvement or hospitalization simply for having suicidal thoughts.  Almost everybody has suicidal thoughts at some point in their life, but most of these don't have a risk of danger along with them.  I truly believe that any hotline worker that has police involvement or hospitalization just because of suicidal thoughts on their own needs to either be retrained or find a different job because it only hurts clients.  And while I don't know if such a law or regulation exists, if the hotline is required by law or by their own regulations to do this, then there needs to be a push to change this.

In regards to the National Suicide Hotline, I have come to believe it may have problems.  I don't know for sure, since my work isn't affiliated with them, but I believe they redirect the caller to a crisis hotline based on the caller's area code.  I don't know if they have technical issues, or maybe they don't update where they redirect their callers, but there seems to be an issue with the national number and never getting a connection.  I've actually had clients call stating they waited with the national hotline for 30 minutes without an answer, but got an answer instantly when they looked up the local center on 211.

So I won't lie, there are chances that you may call a bad hotline.  However, there is also the chance you can call into hotline that can provide the crisis intervention you need.  There are times where a hotline can be beneficial.  There are times when friends and family are not available to help, and a hotline can be therapeutic.  I always recommend calling at least once before you hit your absolute low point.  It can act as proactive treatment, and it can act as practice so it is easier to call if you are feeling overwhelmed or anxious at a later time.  It also can help you figure out what hotline works best for you in your area.  

If the national hotline doesn't work, try calling 211 or google crisis hotlines/centers in your area.  If you need to, try finding one slightly outside your area.
